title: NCERT Maths Book Class 12 Part 2 PDF: What It Covers and How to Study It + Free Quiz
meta_title: NCERT Maths Class 12 Part 2 PDF: Study Guide
meta_desc: How to study NCERT Class 12 Maths Part 2 for boards and JEE: chapter weightage, the best order to attempt, common traps, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Part 2 is where the marks live — Integrals, Vectors, 3-D and Probability carry the bulk of the paper. Here is exactly what the Part 2 PDF contains, the order to attempt it, and the traps that quietly cost students marks. Quick quiz at the end.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Open the NCERT Maths Book Class 12 Part 2 PDF and you are looking at the half of the syllabus that decides your grade. Part 1 has the theory-heavy chapters — Relations, Matrices, Determinants — but Part 2 is where the marks pile up: Integrals, Application of Integrals, Differential Equations, Vector Algebra, Three Dimensional Geometry, Linear Programming and Probability. Roughly 45 of the 80 board marks come from these seven chapters. If your time is short, this is the file to open first.

Below is what each Part 2 chapter actually contains, how heavy it is, and the order I tell students to attempt it. This is not a summary of the book — it is a plan for reading it.

What the NCERT Class 12 Maths Part 2 PDF covers

Part 2 runs from Chapter 7 to Chapter 13. Here is the marks split that has held steady across recent CBSE papers, so you can weight your hours honestly:

ChChapterBoard marks (approx)JEE weight
7Integrals10–12Very high
8Application of Integrals4–6Medium
9Differential Equations5–7High
10Vector Algebra6–7Medium
11Three Dimensional Geometry7–8High
12Linear Programming5Not in JEE
13Probability8High

Notice that Integrals and Probability alone are worth around 20 marks. That table is your revision priority list — do not spread your hours evenly across seven chapters that do not carry equal weight.

The order to attempt Part 2 (this matters)

Chapter number is not study order. The chapters lean on each other, so attempt them in the sequence that builds skill fastest:

  • Integrals first. Everything downstream needs it — you cannot do Application of Integrals or Differential Equations without solid integration.
  • Then Application of Integrals and Differential Equations back to back, while integration is fresh in your hands.
  • Vector Algebra, then 3-D Geometry. Do these as a pair — 3-D is essentially vectors dressed up as lines and planes, and studying them together saves you relearning the dot and cross product twice.
  • Linear Programming and Probability last. Both are self-contained and need no calculus, so they are safe to leave for the end — but do not skip them (see the pitfalls below).

How to study each Part 2 chapter

Integrals (Ch 7)

This is the make-or-break chapter. Do not try to memorise a hundred integrals; learn the four methods — substitution, by parts, partial fractions, and standard forms — and learn to recognise which one a question wants. Work every solved example with a pen before the exercise. In my experience, the students who struggle here skipped the examples and went straight to Exercise 7.2.

Application of Integrals (Ch 8)

Short, high-yield, low-theory. It is almost entirely ‘area under a curve’ problems. Always sketch the region first — the rough figure tells you the limits and whether to integrate with respect to x or y. Students who skip the sketch pick the wrong limits and lose an easy four marks.

Differential Equations (Ch 9)

Two techniques carry the chapter: variable separable and linear (the integrating-factor method). Learn to classify an equation before you solve it — order, degree, and which method applies. The classification step is where board marks are quietly awarded.

Vector Algebra and 3-D Geometry (Ch 10 & 11)

Master the dot product, cross product, and scalar triple product in vectors, and 3-D falls into place — distance between lines, angle between planes, the shortest distance, all of it reuses those three operations. Keep your notation clean; a dropped hat or a sign slip in the cross product is the single most common error I see in this pair.

Linear Programming (Ch 12)

Pure procedure, near-guaranteed marks. Plot the constraints, find the corner points of the feasible region, evaluate the objective function at each. Practise the graph until it is neat — an accurate feasible region is most of the answer.

Probability (Ch 13)

The trap chapter. Conditional probability, Bayes’ theorem and probability distributions look wordy but reward careful reading. Write down what is given and what is asked before touching a formula. Bayes’ theorem in particular is a favourite for the long-answer question.

Common pitfalls that cost marks

  • Treating the PDF as read-only. A book you cannot annotate is a book you will not absorb. Print the chapters you find hard, or keep a rough register keyed to example numbers.
  • Skipping the Miscellaneous Exercises. They are the hardest and the most board-like part of every chapter — and examiners lift questions straight from them.
  • Dropping Linear Programming and Application of Integrals because they ‘feel small.’ Together they are around 10 marks with almost no theory — the cheapest points on the paper.
  • Reading solutions before attempting. It feels like learning; it rarely is. Commit to a full solution first, then check.

A two-week plan for Part 2 before boards

Two focused hours a day beats an all-nighter. A pattern that works: days one to four on Integrals, Application of Integrals and Differential Equations; days five to eight on Vectors and 3-D together; days nine to eleven on Probability and Linear Programming; and the last three days purely on previous-year board and JEE Main questions from these chapters, under a timer. Keep a running list of the questions you could not do unaided — that short list, not the whole PDF, is your final-revision syllabus.

Test yourself on Part 2, then go deeper

Below is a free quiz drawn straight from the Part 2 chapters — integrals, differential equations, vectors, 3-D and probability. Try it, then read the explanations for anything you miss. When you want fully worked, step-by-step solutions to every Part 2 exercise to practise beside the book, the Class 12 Mathematics NCERT Solution Book in the box below gives you exactly that.

quiz.title: NCERT Class 12 Maths Part 2 Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions from the Part 2 chapters — integrals, differential equations, vectors, 3-D geometry and probability. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What is the integral of 1/x dx (for x > 0)?
questions.explanation: The antiderivative of 1/x is the natural logarithm ln|x|, plus the constant of integration C.

questions.q: The area bounded by the curve y = x², the x-axis, and the lines x = 0 and x = 3 is:
questions.explanation: Integrate x² from 0 to 3: [x³/3] gives 27/3 − 0 = 9 square units.

questions.q: What is the order of the differential equation d²y/dx² + 3(dy/dx)³ + y = 0?
questions.explanation: Order is the highest derivative present. The highest here is the second derivative, so the order is 2. The cube affects degree, not order.

questions.q: The dot product of the vectors i + 2j + 3k and 2i + j + k is:
The magnitude of the vector 3i + 4k is:
questions.explanation: Magnitude is the square root of the sum of squares: √(3² + 0² + 4²) = √25 = 5.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4?
questions.explanation: Outcomes greater than 4 are 5 and 6 — two of six equally likely faces, so the probability is 2/6 = 1/3.

questions.q: In linear programming, the maximum or minimum of the objective function occurs at:
options: The centre of the feasible region
A corner point of the feasible region
questions.explanation: By the corner-point theorem, the optimal value of a linear objective function always occurs at a corner (vertex) of the feasible region.

questions.q: The integrating factor of the linear differential equation dy/dx + y = eₓ is:
questions.explanation: For dy/dx + Py = Q, the integrating factor is e raised to the integral of P dx. Here P = 1, so the integrating factor is eₓ.

faq.q: What chapters are in NCERT Class 12 Maths Part 2?
faq.a: Part 2 contains seven chapters: Integrals (Ch 7), Application of Integrals (Ch 8), Differential Equations (Ch 9), Vector Algebra (Ch 10), Three Dimensional Geometry (Ch 11), Linear Programming (Ch 12) and Probability (Ch 13). Together they carry roughly 45 of the 80 board marks.

faq.q: Which Part 2 chapter is the most important?
faq.a: Integrals. It is the single heaviest chapter in the paper and every downstream topic — Application of Integrals and Differential Equations — depends on it. Master the four integration methods before moving on to anything else in Part 2.

faq.q: In what order should I study Part 2?
faq.a: Start with Integrals, then Application of Integrals and Differential Equations while integration is fresh. Do Vector Algebra and 3-D Geometry as a pair, since 3-D reuses vector operations. Finish with Linear Programming and Probability, which need no calculus.

faq.q: Is Part 2 enough for JEE Main as well as boards?
faq.a: Part 2 is the foundation — Integrals, Differential Equations, 3-D and Probability are heavily tested in JEE Main. But NCERT alone is not sufficient for JEE. Finish it first, then drill objective-type and higher-difficulty problems on the same concepts for speed.
